verdicts.trueWording: "can guarantee that all sampled tokens have nonzero true probability" (Abstract)
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in the Abstract (1 occurrence). Every limb holds: Corollary 1 in §3.3 reads that if log p-hat underestimates log p* by at most delta, then for any threshold tau >= 1-exp(-delta), threshold-based truncation correctly discards all tokens not in the support of p*. §3.1 defines that bound as the maximum log-probability underestimation error max(A-A'). Intro restates it. Route: arXiv PDF v1 -> pdftotext -layout, raw page reached.

verdicts.trueWording: "a known source of model errors, the softmax bottleneck" (Abstract)
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in the Abstract. Low-rank limb supported in §2 'The Softmax Bottleneck': limited expressivity of small hidden size with large vocabulary, A' at best a low-rank approximation of A. Caveat on location, not on truth: §2 hedges ('sources are likely many, but one source'); the 'large part' limb is carried by §5.2 Discussion, which reports empirical evidence that the softmax bottleneck is responsible for significant errors in next-token distributions. Cite §5.2 alongside §2 if the magnitude matters.

verdicts.trueWording: "truncating via a threshold is an inherently limited approach" (§4 opening)
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim at the opening of §4. The mechanism limb is the paper's own next clause: if a model assigns more probability to a low quality token than a high quality token, there is no threshold that discards the low-quality one without discarding the high-quality one. Restated in §6 Conclusion.

verdicts.trueWording: "no single method consistently performs best" (§5.1; Figure 5 caption)
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in §5.1 under the heading 'BA-eta outperforms all other methods for GPT-2-Large'. Figure 5 caption independently states no single sampling method consistently outperforms across sizes; the four sizes are Small/Medium/Large/XL and the corpus is the Open Web Text test set, as the claim says.

Quote verbatim. Annotators are Amazon Mechanical Turk workers doing pairwise comparisons (same paragraph). The explanation limb is the paper's next sentence: likely because humans see only one generation per method, making it impossible to assess diversity.

No quotation was offered, so this cannot be graded VERBATIM; every figure matches Table 1 exactly. Table 1 reads eta 85.0(1.4) Small, 90.4 Medium, 86.0 Large, 87.1(1.2) XL; BA-eta 87.8(1.0), 92.2, 88.4, 89.6(0.4). Caption: MAUVE scores for different GPT-2 model sizes on lower-entropy OWT generation. Subscripts are standard deviations the claim omits.

verdicts.trueWording: "few consecutive sentence-level repetitions in human corpora (e.g., 0.02% in Wikitext-103)"
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in the Abstract. The contrast limb is the same Abstract sentence pair: models get stuck in sentence-level loops with maximization-based decoding (e.g., greedy search), which the authors call counter-intuitive against the human 0.02%. Note for the merger: Table 1 lists human Repetition-Sen as 0.01% on the Wikitext-103 test set, a different measurement from the Abstract's corpus figure, not a contradiction.

verdicts.trueWording: "the more times a sentence is repeated in the context" (Abstract)
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim; the full Abstract finding 2 names it the self-reinforcement effect and continues 'of continuing to generate that sentence'. Restated in §2.2 under 'Why the model gets stuck into the repetition loop?', which adds that IP, WR and TP converge around ceiling values.

verdicts.trueWording: "IP1 is higher than 90% across the various corpus" (§2.2)
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim (2 occurrences: §1 and §2.2). IP is defined in §2.1 as the Rate of Increased Token Probability, the share of tokens whose probability rises versus the first sentence, so 'more than ninety per cent of tokens' is the right reading. The final limb is the paper's own note: the token repetition has not occurred at the current prediction step, only the same sentence-level context.

verdicts.trueWording: "The sentences with higher initial probabilities usually have a stronger self-reinforcement"
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in Abstract finding 3. The maximisation-decoding limb is §2.2 'What kinds of sentences are more likely to be repeated?': sentences generated by a maximization-based decoding algorithm have higher initial likelihoods, thus the model prefers to repeat itself. §1 states the same with a hedge ('may have a stronger self-reinforcement effect'); the claim's 'most at risk of looping' is firmer than §1 but matches §2.2.

verdicts.trueWording: "chosen with maximum probability which can avoid the self-reinforcement effect" (§2.2)
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in §2.2 'Analyses'. Two points of nuance the claim smooths over: the paper hedges ('The effectiveness ... may rely on'), and it gives two reasons, of which the claim states only the second; the first is that previously generated sentences carry lower likelihood under stochastic sampling and so are less at risk of repetition.

No quotation was offered, so not gradable as VERBATIM; both figures match Table 1 exactly. Table 1 caption: results of different training-based methods on the test set of Wikitext-103 for open-ended generation, and §4.2 states these comparisons are based on greedy decoding, supporting 'greedy-style decoding'. MLE is the maximum-likelihood baseline. Repetition-Sen is defined in §4.1 as 1 - unique sentences / sentences.

verdicts.trueWording: "language models do look at the long-distance context" (§1)
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in §1 Introduction. Both limbs hold: the sentence runs against Fu et al., named in the preceding sentence as assuming language models can be approximated by short-sighted first-order Markov models, and rests on Holtzman et al.'s observed cases of a positive feedback loop of repetitions. Repeated in the Related Work section. Polarity 'disputes' is correct.

verdicts.trueWording: "top-k sampling, and nucleus sampling are all inconsistent" (after Theorem 3.4)
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in the paragraph immediately after Theorem 3.4. The zero-probability limb is the Abstract's definition of inconsistency: the algorithm can yield an infinite-length sequence that has zero probability under the model, and the Abstract states the same four algorithms are proven inconsistent.

verdicts.trueWording: Table 4: GPT2-117M rL 37.91%, greedy decoding, limit L = 500
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'had not ended within 1500 steps' - the 37.91% figure is measured at L = 500, not 1500
verdicts.note: 37.91 is exact in Table 4 for GPT2-117M, greedy-decoded, Wikitext-103, and rL is defined in §5 as the proportion of decoded continuations at least L tokens long, so the 'share of contexts' reading is right. But §5.3 states explicitly that this experiment defines the non-termination ratio using L = 500, 'more strict than the limit used in the preceding experiments (1500)'; 1500 belongs to the earlier recurrent-LM experiments (Table 1), not to Table 4. Downstream text should say 500 steps.
